lead: This unit teaches how a machine part is conceived, sized and checked before it is drawn. You will learn the design process, material choice, standard fits, safety factors and the stress equations for direct, bending, torsional, combined and curved-beam loading. After it you can read a simple design problem, choose a safe trial section and check it for strength and stiffness.
about: The unit starts with the design process in 1.1 and the factors that shape a machine part. 1.2 turns those factors into a material choice using mechanical properties. 1.3 fixes standard sizes, fits and tolerances; 1.4 adds factor of safety and design codes. 1.5 classifies static, dynamic and impact loads, and 1.6 gives the three basic stress equations. 1.7 combines stresses and finds principal stresses, including eccentric loading. 1.8 uses strength and stiffness checks to choose dimensions, and 1.9 extends the bending idea to curved beams such as crane hooks and C-frames.

chapters.idea: Design is a loop from need to tested product, and every choice balances function, strength, cost and manufacturability.
chapters.depth: Cover the stages: need recognition, specification, concept, embodiment, detail, prototype and production; show the feedback loops. Discuss factors that shape a design: load and duty, material and manufacturing, cost and batch size, safety and codes, environment and maintenance, ergonomics, reliability and legal limits. Some syllabi call this introduction to design. Keep the treatment qualitative; numerical work starts in 1.3 and 1.6.

figure.title: Design loop
figure.aria: A design moves from need and specification through concept and detail to a prototype; the prototype test sends revisions back to the concept.

chapters.example: A small Chennai workshop needs a wall bracket for an 8 kg ceiling fan. The bracket must last 5 years, the batch is 200 pieces, the workshop has manual milling and welding, and the target cost is ₹250 per bracket. List the design stages, name four factors that control the design, and give one design decision for each factor.
chapters.trap: Treating design as a fixed sequence; testing usually sends the team back to concept or detail, and cost or manufacturing can control the final choice.
chapters.leave: Detailed stress analysis to later chapters; standards to 1.4.

chapters.idea: Choose a material by matching its property vector to the likely failure mode and the manufacturing process, not by one strength number.
chapters.depth: Link properties to failure mode: yield strength for static ductile failure, ultimate strength for brittle fracture, fatigue strength for repeated load, hardness for wear, toughness for shock, stiffness E for deflection, plus density, corrosion, machinability, weldability and cost. Compare plain carbon steel, alloy steel, cast iron, aluminium and copper alloys, and common plastics. Mention Ashby selection charts; only a few universities teach selection indices, so keep them to one line.

figure.aria: A decision tree matches the likely failure mode to a candidate material, such as yielding to plain carbon steel and wear to hardened steel.

chapters.example: Select a material for a lever that carries 2.5 kN at 300 mm from the pivot. The allowable bending stress is 120 MPa, so the required section modulus is 6.25×10³ mm³. Plain carbon steel has S_y = 250 MPa, density 7850 kg/m³ and cost ₹70/kg; aluminium alloy has S_y = 280 MPa, density 2700 kg/m³ and cost ₹320/kg. Which material is safe for a factor of safety 2 on yield, and for equal volume which is lighter and which costs less?
chapters.trap: Choosing by yield strength alone; a light alloy may be strong enough but too flexible because E is lower, and a hard surface may hide a brittle core.
chapters.leave: Fatigue strength and failure theories to Unit 2; detailed material processing to manufacturing courses.

chapters.idea: Preferred numbers, fits and tolerances standardize sizes and clearances so interchangeable parts can be made at acceptable cost.
chapters.depth: Cover preferred numbers R5, R10, R20 and R40; basic size, actual size, limits, tolerance, allowance; clearance, interference and transition fits; hole-basis and shaft-basis systems; common ISO IT grades and fits such as H7/g6. Show how a tolerance stack changes cost. Some syllabi call tolerance the permissible variation. Do not derive ISO tables; use the standard values.

figure.title: Preferred numbers, one decade
figure.aria: The R5 and R10 preferred-number rows give rounded standard sizes for one decade; the R10 row is denser than the R5 row.

chapters.example: A nominal 25 mm hole and shaft have hole limits 25.000 mm and 25.021 mm, and shaft limits 24.980 mm and 24.993 mm. Find the hole tolerance, shaft tolerance, allowance, maximum clearance and minimum clearance, and name the fit.
chapters.trap: Calling allowance the same as clearance; allowance is the minimum clearance or maximum interference planned, not the actual gap after tolerances. Also watch hole-basis versus shaft-basis letters.
chapters.leave: Detailed selection of bearings and gears with fits to Units 5 and 7.

chapters.idea: Factor of safety converts uncertain strength into an allowable stress, while design codes fix minimum rules and calculation methods.
chapters.depth: Define factor of safety on yield, ultimate and fatigue strength. Separate factors for load uncertainty, material uncertainty and consequence of failure. Show n = S/σ_allow and the check σ_actual ≤ σ_allow. Explain design codes as mandatory rules that set minimum safety and calculation methods; codes are not the same as FoS. Name ASME, IS and ISO as examples. Theories of failure are Unit 2.

figure.aria: Factor of safety turns a measured strength into an allowable stress, which is then compared with the calculated stress.

chapters.example: A ductile steel tie has yield strength 280 MPa and cross-section 250 mm². The expected tensile load is 45 kN. Using a factor of safety 2.5 on yield, find the allowable stress, the actual stress and the ratio of actual to allowable; state whether the design is safe.
chapters.trap: Using ultimate strength for a ductile part that would fail by yielding; or applying one global FoS when a code requires separate load and resistance factors.
chapters.leave: Failure theories and fatigue criteria to Unit 2; shaft code equations to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: Load classification by time sets the analysis method: static is steady, dynamic repeats or reverses, and impact is a sudden energy input.
chapters.depth: Classify loads by time: static or steady, dynamic or fluctuating, and impact or shock. Show that a suddenly applied constant load gives about twice the static stress in a linear elastic member. For impact use energy: falling weight, strain energy and dynamic factor. Repeated fatigue loading is Unit 2. Some syllabi call impact loading shock loading.

figure.aria: Load-time histories compare a steady static load, a repeating dynamic load and a sharp impact spike.

chapters.example: A 10 kg weight falls 100 mm onto a collar at the lower end of a vertical steel bar. The bar is 1 m long, 500 mm² in area and E = 200 GPa. Find the maximum stress by the energy method and compare it with the stress if the same weight is applied gradually.
chapters.trap: Multiplying a falling weight by a guessed impact factor instead of using energy; also forgetting that a sudden load is not the same as a falling load.
chapters.leave: Fatigue life and S-N curves to Unit 2; impact tests and fracture to materials courses.

chapters.idea: Internal force resultants produce three basic stress distributions: uniform direct stress, linear bending stress and torsional shear stress.
chapters.depth: Derive or state σ = P/A for direct stress, σ = My/I for bending and τ = Tr/J for torsion in a circular shaft. Define A area, P axial force, M bending moment, y distance from neutral axis, I second moment of area, T torque, r radius, J polar second moment. Introduce section modulus Z = I/y and polar modulus J/r. State assumptions: linear elastic, small deflection, plane sections remain plane.

figure.aria: The three internal resultants produce a uniform axial stress, a linear bending stress and a radial torsional shear stress.

chapters.example: A 40 mm diameter solid shaft carries an axial compressive load of 30 kN, a bending moment of 600 N·m and a torque of 450 N·m. Calculate the direct stress, the maximum bending stress and the maximum torsional shear stress at the surface.
chapters.trap: Using diameter instead of radius in Tr/J, or adding a bending stress at one point to a torsional shear stress as if they were the same type.
chapters.prereq: 1.5 for load type; basic mechanics for area and second moment.
chapters.leave: Stress concentration to Unit 2; shaft design to Unit 3; shear stress distribution in non-circular sections to mechanics.

chapters.idea: Real members carry combined stresses; eccentric loads add direct and bending stresses, and principal stresses identify the critical planes.
chapters.depth: Combine normal stresses from axial load and bending, and shear from torsion. For an eccentric load, replace the offset force by a direct force at the centroid plus a moment. Use σ1,2 = (σx+σy)/2 ± √(((σx−σy)/2)² + τ²) and τmax = √(((σx−σy)/2)² + τ²). Show Mohr's circle for a two-dimensional state. Some syllabi call this calculation of principal stresses for load combinations.

figure.aria: An eccentric load is split into direct and bending stresses; these form a stress state whose principal stresses are found and checked.

chapters.example: A 50 mm diameter solid shaft transmits 15 kW at 300 rpm and carries a bending moment of 800 N·m. Find the torsional shear stress, the bending stress at the surface and the two principal stresses. Use π = 3.142.
chapters.trap: Adding principal stresses to shear stresses, or forgetting that an eccentric load always creates a moment as well as a direct force.
chapters.leave: Three-dimensional states and yield theories to Unit 2; eccentric bolted and welded joints to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A safe part must pass two checks: strength against stress and stiffness against deflection or twist.
chapters.depth: Set two checks: strength, σmax ≤ S/FoS, and stiffness, δmax ≤ δallow or θmax ≤ θallow. Use δ = PL/AE for axial, standard beam deflection formulas for bending, and θ = TL/GJ for torsion. Choose a trial section, check strength, then stiffness, and resize if either fails. Mention that stiffness often controls long shafts and slender beams. Simple machine parts only.

figure.aria: A trial section passes a strength check and then a stiffness check; either failure sends the designer back to resize.

chapters.example: A simply supported steel beam of span 1.2 m carries a central load of 10 kN. The allowable bending stress is 120 MPa, the allowable deflection is 3 mm, and E = 200 GPa. The section is rectangular with depth h = 2b. Choose the smallest width b that satisfies both checks.
chapters.trap: Checking strength only; a part can be strong enough and still fail because deflection or twist exceeds the limit.
chapters.leave: Critical speed and shaft rigidity details to Unit 3; complex beam deflection methods to mechanics.

chapters.idea: In a curved beam the neutral axis shifts toward the centre of curvature, so bending stress is hyperbolic and highest at the inner fibre.
chapters.depth: Explain why the neutral axis shifts toward the centre of curvature in a curved beam. For a rectangular section use R_n = h/ln(R_o/R_i), e = R − R_n, and σ = M(R_n − r)/(A e r), with M positive when it increases curvature; positive stress is tensile at the inner fibre. Cover crane hooks and C-frames. Stress concentration at the inner fibre is Unit 2.

figure.aria: Curved-beam stress is highest at the inner fibre and falls hyperbolically; a straight-beam stress would change linearly.

chapters.example: A crane hook carries 20 kN. Its cross-section is rectangular: width 30 mm, depth 60 mm. The inner radius is 40 mm. Find the maximum tensile stress at the inner fibre and the maximum compressive stress at the outer fibre using curved-beam theory.
chapters.trap: Using the straight-beam formula σ = My/I for a deeply curved member; the error is large when the depth is comparable with the radius.
chapters.leave: Stress concentration and fatigue of hooks to Unit 2; hook standards and threads to Unit 4.
